content_html:
Asset allocation is how a portfolio is divided between broad types of investment, such as stocks, bonds and cash. The mix tends to shape both the long-run growth and the size of the swings far more than any single holding. This calculator does not tell you what mix to hold. It shows where you stand today, what it would take to reach a mix you choose, and how mixes compare under assumptions that you set and can change at any time.

How to use this calculator

  1. Current value: what you hold in each asset class now, across all accounts you want to include. Use Other assets for anything that does not fit the first three, such as real estate funds.
  2. Target mix: the percentage you want to test in each class. The targets must add up to 100%.
  3. Hypothetical return: an assumed average yearly return for each class. The starting figures are placeholders for illustration only.
  4. Hypothetical bad year: an assumed change in a single poor year, used to illustrate how a mix might react to a downturn.
  5. Monthly addition and years: how much you plan to add and how long to project.

How the results are worked out

  • Current mix: each class's value divided by the portfolio total.
  • Change to reach the target: the target percentage times the total, minus what you hold now. Positive amounts are added to a class and negative amounts taken out; together they always net to $0.
  • Blended return: each class's hypothetical return weighted by its share of the mix. For example, 60% at 7%, 30% at 4% and 10% at 2% blends to 5.6%.
  • Projection: today's total plus monthly additions, growing at the blended return as if the mix were rebalanced back to its weights along the way.
  • Bad year: each class's hypothetical change weighted by its share, applied to today's total.

Worked example with the starting figures

The starting figures describe a $100,000 portfolio holding $70,000 in stocks, $22,000 in bonds and $8,000 in cash, tested against a 60/30/10 target. These are sample numbers, not a suggested mix.

MeasureCurrent mix (70/22/8)Target mix (60/30/10)
Blended hypothetical return5.94%5.6%
Projected value after 20 years with $500 a month$542,306$514,185
Hypothetical bad year today−$22,100−$19,500

Reaching the target here means moving $10,000 out of stocks, adding $8,000 to bonds and $2,000 to cash. Under these sample assumptions, the current mix projects a higher balance and a deeper bad-year drop. That trade-off between growth and swings is the core of allocation; change the assumptions and the numbers change with them.

Important limits

  • The returns and bad-year figures are hypothetical. Nobody knows future returns, and real portfolios rarely grow in a straight line.
  • The projection ignores taxes, fees and the costs of rebalancing, such as capital gains tax on sales in a taxable account.
  • Asset classes do not always move in step, so a real downturn can affect a mix differently from a simple weighted average.
  • This tool is for education and illustration. It is not investment advice and does not consider your goals, timeline or tolerance for risk. A licensed financial professional can help with personal decisions.

faq.question: Where do the starting return figures come from?
faq.answer: They are round placeholder numbers chosen only to make the example work, not estimates or forecasts. Replace them with your own assumptions, or try several sets to see how sensitive the results are.

faq.question: Why might the projected values differ so much between mixes?
faq.answer: Small differences in a yearly return compound over many years. Because the projection uses a steady rate, it shows that effect clearly, but it does not show the ups and downs a real portfolio would go through along the way.

faq.question: Can I rebalance with new money instead of selling?
faq.answer: Yes. The change column shows the end point. You could direct future additions toward the classes that are below target instead of selling, which can avoid triggering taxes in a taxable account, though it takes longer.

faq.question: Do I need to fill in Other assets?
faq.answer: No. Leave its current value and target at 0 if you do not use it. You can also rename it in your head to any class you track separately, such as real estate or international stocks.

faq.question: Does this calculator recommend an allocation?
faq.answer: No. It only compares mixes you enter using assumptions you control. It does not consider your age, goals or circumstances, and it is not investment advice.
